target: Agent 1’s claim that animal dissection is acceptable because over 98% of dissected animals were already dead and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: In practice, dissection is often supplied by animals caught in the wild, so it is not mainly a harmless repurposing of already-dead carcasses; it can instead depend on inhumane capture that harms biodiversity.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection should be part of biology education because it offers valuable learning.
objection: Dissection is not required by AP Biology, Next Generation Science Standards, or physician training in U.S. and Canadian medical schools, so it is not necessary to meet core curriculum or training goals.

target: Agent 1’s claim that real-animal dissection is educationally necessary.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach anatomy and biological structure as well as or better than dead animals, so students can learn just as well without dissecting real animals.

target: Agent 2’s suggestion that refusing dissection meaningfully prevents animal deaths because animals are being newly killed for class use.
objection: If classroom dissection uses animals that were already dead, then not dissecting them does not save those animals’ lives; it mostly just changes how already-dead carcasses are disposed of.

target: Agent 2’s underlying assumption that dissection of dead specimens requires additional killing of living animals.
objection: When the practice mainly repurposes already-dead carcasses, it does not involve new killing in the way the objection assumes, so the welfare concern is weakened.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection-specimen supply is effectively fixed and unaffected by classroom demand.
objection: If schools require specimens for repeated use, then increasing demand will usually cause suppliers to source more animals, so classroom dissection tends to increase the number of animals killed or captured.

target: Agent 1’s claim that using dead byproducts means dissection is not environmentally or ethically problematic.
objection: Because dissection specimens are often sourced through wild capture, increasing dissection demand can still increase inhumane, biodiversity-damaging harm rather than merely using existing byproducts.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection demand increases animal deaths because specimen supply is demand-driven.
objection: Classroom dissection specimens are largely already-dead meat-industry byproducts, so they are not necessarily sourced from animals killed or captured specifically for classroom demand.

target: Agent 2’s assumption that classroom demand controls specimen production.
objection: If the animals are byproducts of the meat industry, then their upstream production is driven by meat-industry processes rather than by classroom demand, making the supply effectively independent of school use.

target: Agent 2’s claim that school dissection creates environmental harm because fixatives and biological waste are hazardous.
objection: Hazardous fixatives and biological waste can be handled through licensed hazardous-waste disposal, which substantially prevents environmental release and means dissection does not necessarily cause major environmental harm.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives make dissection unnecessary.
objection: Dissection provides substantial educational value, including hands-on biology learning, fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and career inspiration, so it is not merely redundant.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection mainly increases animal deaths beyond the meat supply chain.
objection: Classroom dissection can use carcasses and byproducts that would otherwise be discarded or landfilled, so choosing dissection may mainly repurpose existing specimens rather than cause new deaths.

target: Agent 1’s claim that classroom dissection mostly uses already-dead byproducts and therefore does not add much harm.
objection: Most dissection animals are reportedly caught in the wild, so choosing dissection can increase wild capture and deaths rather than merely repurposing meat-industry waste.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that there is no evidence dissection choice increases animal deaths beyond the meat supply chain.
objection: That assumption is false because dissection demand can increase wild-catching deaths and captures beyond what would happen from the meat supply chain alone.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives provide equivalent learning outcomes.
objection: Fine motor skills and tactile hand-eye coordination require physical manipulation of real materials, and simulations may not provide the same hands-on experience, so equivalence is not established.
